summary:
The Spirit Lake Tribe is a Dakota nation. Its people call themselves Mni Wakan Oyate, the people of the Spirit Water, after the Dakota name for the lake along the reservation's northern edge. Most families descend from the Sisseton and Wahpeton bands, along with Cut Head Yanktonai people who were already settled in the area.

After the 1862 war in Minnesota, many Dakota moved west into Dakota Territory. An 1867 treaty set aside land for Sisseton and Wahpeton families between Devils Lake and the Sheyenne River. The Army built Fort Totten there the same year. When the soldiers left in 1890, the post became a government boarding school for reservation children.

Allotment broke the reservation into individual parcels starting in the late 1880s, and in 1904 the remaining land was opened to outside settlers. Today most of the land inside the boundaries is no longer held by the tribe or its members.

The nation was long known as the Devils Lake Sioux Tribe and took the name Spirit Lake late in the twentieth century. Tribal headquarters is at Fort Totten, which is also home to Cankdeska Cikana Community College, where Dakota language and culture are taught alongside degree programs.

summary:
MHA Nation brings together three peoples: the Mandan (Nueta), the Hidatsa, and the Arikara (Sahnish). The Mandan and Hidatsa speak Siouan languages, and Sahnish is a Caddoan language. All three lived in villages along the Missouri River, where they farmed the bottomlands.

Smallpox struck the villages again and again. The 1837 epidemic left very few Mandan alive. Mandan and Hidatsa survivors built Like-a-Fishhook village together, and the Sahnish later joined them there. The 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie recognized more than 12 million acres as MHA land. An 1870 executive order and later federal actions, made without the nation's consent, cut that down to the present Fort Berthold Reservation in west-central North Dakota.

The hardest blow came from Garrison Dam, which Congress authorized in 1944. Its reservoir flooded more than 150,000 acres of the nation's best bottomland in the early 1950s. The agency town of Elbowoods was lost, along with homes, schools, the hospital, and the tribal headquarters. Families were moved from fertile river land to the uplands.

Today the tribal government sits in New Town, which is also home to Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College.

summary:
The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians is home to Chippewa people and to Métis families, who descend from Chippewa women and French and English fur traders. In North Dakota the Métis are part of the band. The reservation sits in the Turtle Mountains near the Canadian border, a rolling country of woods, lakes, and streams.

The band's ancestors once held a vast territory across northern Dakota. In 1863, at Old Crossing on the Red Lake River, Chippewa leaders including Little Shell met federal negotiators who wanted land along the Red River. In 1882 a presidential executive order created a large reservation in the Turtle Mountains, but it was soon cut to a block of just two townships.

The band's claim to its wider homeland was settled through the McCumber Agreement. The federal government negotiated it with a council picked by the government's agent, not by the people. Little Shell refused to sign and protested in Washington. The deal paid about ten cents an acre, which is why many remember it as the Ten Cent Treaty. Some families were later given land near Trenton in western North Dakota, now a tribal service area.

Tribal headquarters is in Belcourt, also home to Turtle Mountain Community College.

summary:
The Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate are Dakota people of the Sisitunwan and Wahpetunwan bands, part of the eastern, or Santee, Dakota. Before the 1860s their families lived along the Minnesota River in present-day Minnesota.

After years of land cessions, a treaty signed in 1867 set aside the Lake Traverse Reservation. It is a triangle of land in northeastern South Dakota that reaches into southeastern North Dakota. In 1891 a federal law ratified an agreement with the bands and opened land inside the reservation to non-Native settlers. In 1975 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the 1891 law had ended the reservation's original boundaries. Three justices dissented. The nation has not accepted that outcome, and its leaders continue to press for the 1867 boundaries to be recognized again.

The tribal government reorganized in 1946 and has been based at Agency Village ever since. For decades the nation was known as the Sisseton-Wahpeton Sioux Tribe. Tribal voters later chose the name Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate. The nation's tribal college, Sisseton Wahpeton College, serves students on the reservation.

summary:
The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe is home to Lakota and Dakota people. They include the Hunkpapa and Sihasapa bands of the Lakota and the Upper and Lower Yanktonai (Ihanktonwana and Hunkpatina) of the Dakota. The reservation straddles the North Dakota–South Dakota line on the west side of the Missouri River.

Standing Rock was once part of the Great Sioux Reservation, which the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie set out across all of present-day South Dakota west of the Missouri. A federal agency opened at Fort Yates in 1873. In 1877 Congress took the Black Hills without the consent of three-fourths of adult men that the treaty required. In 1889 another act broke the remaining land into separate reservations and opened much of it to settlers, and Standing Rock's boundaries come from that act. The Hunkpapa leader Sitting Bull is among the nation's best-known members.

Later, the reservoir behind Oahe Dam flooded the reservation's Missouri River bottomlands and timber.

Tribal headquarters is at Fort Yates, North Dakota, also home to Sitting Bull College. In North Dakota, all of Sioux County lies within the reservation.

summary:
The Oglala Sioux Tribe is the government of the Oglala Lakota, one of the Lakota bands of the Oceti Sakowin. Its homeland, the Pine Ridge Reservation, covers about 1.7 million acres in southwestern South Dakota.

In the 1860s the Oglala leader Red Cloud led the fight to close the Bozeman Trail through Lakota hunting country. That war ended with the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which recognized a Great Sioux Reservation across all of present-day South Dakota west of the Missouri River. In 1877 the United States took the Black Hills, and in 1889 Congress divided what was left into smaller reservations, Pine Ridge among them.

The Oglala agency began near Fort Laramie in present-day Wyoming. It moved several times before settling at Pine Ridge. In December 1890, U.S. troops killed Lakota men, women, and children at Wounded Knee, a massacre that ended the era of armed conflict between the Lakota and the United States.

Tribal government is based in the town of Pine Ridge. Oglala Lakota College, based in Kyle, serves communities across the reservation. Red Cloud's push for a school at Pine Ridge led to what is now Red Cloud Indian School.

summary:
The Rosebud Sioux Tribe is the Sicangu Lakota Oyate, the Burnt Thigh People. They descend from the Sicangu of the Tetonwan (Lakota) division of the Oceti Sakowin, the Seven Council Fires. The nation's history describes Lakota ancestors living in and around present-day Minnesota before pressure from the Ojibwe pushed them west onto the plains. There they became horseback buffalo hunters.

Chief Spotted Tail, Sinte Gleska in Lakota, led the Sicangu through the treaty years and signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. The Sicangu agency moved many times, along the Missouri River and into northwestern Nebraska. Spotted Tail sought to move it away from the whiskey trade on the river. It finally settled on Rosebud Creek near the South Fork of the White River, named for the wild roses on its banks. When Congress divided the Great Sioux Reservation in 1889, Rosebud became a separate reservation.

Today the reservation lies in south-central South Dakota along the Nebraska line. Tribal headquarters is in Rosebud. Sinte Gleska University, which carries Spotted Tail's Lakota name, is based in nearby Mission.

summary:
The Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe is a Lakota nation made up of four bands, or tiospaye: the Mnicoujou, Itazipco, Siha Sapa, and Oohenumpa. Its reservation lies in north-central South Dakota. The Missouri River forms its eastern edge, and the Cheyenne and Moreau rivers cross it.

The four bands were part of the Great Sioux Reservation set out by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. A federal agency served them from the west bank of the Missouri. When Congress broke up the Great Sioux Reservation in 1889, Cheyenne River became a separate reservation. Big Foot, a Mnicoujou leader, was among those killed at Wounded Knee in December 1890.

In the 1950s the Missouri River dam program reshaped the reservation. The reservoir behind Oahe Dam flooded most of the reservation's timbered river bottomland, including the Cheyenne River Agency itself. The agency and its services had to move inland. The federal government considered several sites, and the tribe rebuilt its headquarters at Eagle Butte, near the center of the reservation.

Eagle Butte remains the seat of tribal government and home to Cheyenne River College Center.

summary:
The Lower Brule Sioux Tribe calls itself Kul Wicasa Oyate, the Lower People. They are Sicangu Lakota, part of the Tetonwan nation. Long ago the Sicangu divided into the Kul Wicasa and the Heyata Wicasa, the upland people. The name Brule comes from French traders' translation of Sicangu.

Chief Iron Nation led the people through some of their hardest years. He signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which set out the Great Sioux Reservation. A federal agency was set up on the west bank of the Missouri River, across from Crow Creek, and the Lower Brule Reservation took shape there in what are now Lyman and Stanley counties.

The Missouri River dams of the 1950s and 1960s hit the nation twice. Fort Randall Dam's reservoir flooded sheltered bottomland pasture. Big Bend Dam took more land and forced the town of Lower Brule itself to move about a mile west. Between them the two dams put much of the tribe's forests, hunting, fishing and gathering grounds, farmland, and settlements under Lake Francis Case and Lake Sharpe.

Tribal government is based in Lower Brule, which is also home to Lower Brule Community College.

summary:
The Crow Creek Sioux Tribe lives on the east bank of the Missouri River in central South Dakota. Its people are Dakota, descended largely from the Hunkpati, or Lower Yanktonai, along with Mdewakanton families.

The reservation dates to 1863. After the 1862 war in Minnesota, the federal government removed Dakota people, along with Winnebago families, to Crow Creek. The land was strange to them and produced little food. Supplies were short, and many people died of hunger and exposure. In 1866 the surviving Dakota were moved again, to a new reservation in Nebraska. Lower Yanktonai people settled at the agency, and the band of Drifting Goose later gave up its own small reservation on the James River and joined them.

The Missouri River dams of the 1950s and 1960s brought another hard chapter. Fort Randall and Big Bend dams flooded thousands of acres of the tribe's river bottomland, and the community of Fort Thompson was flooded and had to be relocated. The federal agency and hospital were moved off the reservation, and the Fort Thompson boarding school closed.

Fort Thompson remains the tribal headquarters and the reservation's largest community.

summary:
The Yankton Sioux Tribe is the Ihanktonwan Oyate, the People of the End Village. Their reservation lies on the north bank of the Missouri River in Charles Mix County, in southeastern South Dakota.

Struck by the Ree and other headmen spent months in Washington, D.C., negotiating a treaty with the United States. Signed on April 19, 1858, it gave up more than 11 million acres and set aside a reservation along the Missouri. The people moved onto it the following year, and the federal agency was set up at Greenwood.

Allotment divided the reservation into individual parcels, and much of the land passed out of Ihanktonwan hands. Today the tribe's land is scattered across the original reservation rather than held in one block. In the twentieth century Fort Randall Dam's reservoir, Lake Francis Case, covered part of the reservation's southwest and submerged the White Swan community.

Tribal headquarters is in Wagner. Ihanktonwan Community College serves tribal members, and the Marty Indian School continues on the reservation.

summary:
The Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribe is a Dakota nation. Its members descend from the Mdewakantonwan, with Wahpekute relatives, eastern Dakota people whose homeland lay in present-day Minnesota.

The Santee gave up most of their land in treaties and moved onto a reservation in Minnesota. The nation's history describes the government failing to meet its treaty promises while traders held back food, and war broke out in 1862. Afterward the Dakota were held in camps and then removed, first to Crow Creek in Dakota Territory and later to the Santee Agency in Nebraska.

In 1869, 25 families left the Santee Agency. They gave up their tribal annuities to become citizens and took homesteads along the Big Sioux River, in what became Flandreau, South Dakota. Fifteen more families joined them that fall. Their community, which built one of the state's oldest Presbyterian churches still in use, became the foundation of today's tribe. In the 1930s it organized its government under the Indian Reorganization Act.

The tribe is based in Flandreau, in Moody County. The federally run Flandreau Indian School, a boarding school, still operates there.
